title: Lima beans and corn, cooked, fat added

content.title: About
content.content: Lima beans (also called butter beans) and corn cooked together with added fat form a nutritious dish commonly used in stews, soups, and side dishes. Lima beans are large, creamy‑textured, while corn adds sweetness and a crunchy bite. The fat—usually a vegetable oil or butter—enhances flavor and helps absorb fat‑soluble vitamins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lima beans are native to South America and were cultivated by the Inca civilization.
Corn was domesticated over 7,000 years ago in Mexico and became a staple crop throughout the Americas.
Combining beans and corn creates a complete protein profile, as the amino acids complement each other.
Traditional Native American recipes often paired these two crops because they were grown side by side.
Adding a small amount of fat increases the bioavailability of corn’s carotenoids.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Lima beans provide about 7 g of protein per 100 g, and corn adds another 3 g, making the dish a good protein source for vegetarians.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: The bean‑corn combination supplies over 5 g of fiber per serving, supporting digestive health.

items.title: Source of vitamin B6 and folate
items.content: Vitamin B6 aids amino‑acid metabolism, while folate is essential for DNA synthesis and cell growth.

items.title: Contains iron and magnesium
items.content: Lima beans are a decent source of iron (≈2 mg/100 g) and magnesium, which are important for energy production and muscle function.

items.title: Corn antioxidants
items.content: Yellow corn is rich in lutein and zeaxanthin, antioxidants that protect eye health.

items.title: Allergy to legumes or corn
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to lima beans or corn.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Because the dish is prepared with added fat, its calorie density is higher; portion control is advised for weight‑management.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Beans contain phytic acid, which can reduce mineral absorption; soaking before cooking lowers its level.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Legumes can cause gastrointestinal gas in sensitive people; introduce them gradually.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the beans and corn as a side dish, stir them into soups, chili, salads, or use them in casseroles. Cook the beans until tender, then sauté with a modest amount of oil and add the corn in the last few minutes to keep it crisp.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cooked dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Frozen portions retain quality for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C before serving.
